morning.title: IAF’s MTA Tender Demands Proof of Carrying Zorawar Light Tank, M777 Howitzers, and BrahMos Canisters
morning.text:
Bidders competing for India’s 80-aircraft Medium Transport Aircraft (MTA) tender will need to demonstrate their aircraft can physically carry some of the Indian military’s heaviest and most sensitive mobile hardware — including the indigenous 25-tonne Zorawar light tank, M777 ultra-light howitzers, BrahMos missile canisters, and Akash air-defence launcher units — according to sources close to idrw.org. The requirement sets a demanding technical bar as the tender moves toward formal issuance, and it directly shapes which of the competing aircraft can realistically qualify.
The Payload Requirements in Detail
The IAF requires the MTA to carry payloads ranging from 18 to 30 tonnes, with the cargo bay capable of accommodating light armoured vehicles including the indigenous 25-tonne Zorawar light tank, artillery systems such as the M777 ultra-light howitzer, BrahMos missile canisters, and Akash air-defence launcher units. The aircraft must also support logistics operations along the northern and eastern borders, including Ladakh and Arunachal Pradesh, with a critical requirement being the ability to land and take off from short, unprepared airstrips, alongside low-altitude operation capability and advanced night-navigation systems for covert troop insertion and extraction.
This is a notably specific and demanding list. Rather than a generic “18-30 tonne payload” specification, the IAF has tied the requirement directly to named platforms already in service or entering service — meaning bidders can’t simply claim generic payload capacity on paper; they’ll need to demonstrate actual physical and dimensional compatibility with these exact systems.
Why the Zorawar Requirement Matters So Much
The Zorawar is a 25-tonne indigenous light tank developed by Larsen & Toubro alongside DRDO’s Combat Vehicles Research and Development Establishment, designed specifically for high-altitude operations in terrain like Ladakh where heavier platforms such as the T-72, T-90, and Arjun struggle with mobility. DRDO Chief Dr Samir V Kamat has confirmed that Army user trials of the Zorawar will begin this year, with an initial order of 59 tanks expected once trials conclude successfully, followed by a much larger tender for around 350 additional units.
Given that Zorawar’s entire strategic purpose is rapid mobility to remote, high-altitude sectors, the ability to airlift it via the MTA fleet isn’t a nice-to-have — it’s central to how the Army intends to actually employ the tank operationally. A light tank that can’t be airlifted quickly to a contested high-altitude sector loses much of its strategic value over simply road-marching heavier armour, which defeats the purpose of building a dedicated light tank in the first place.
What This Means for the Competing Aircraft
Three prominent international contenders are currently vying for the multi-billion-dollar MTA contract, each tailoring bids to India’s indigenisation requirements: Embraer’s C-390M Millennium partnering with Mahindra Defence, alongside other Western options, while a Russian IL-276 proposal with HAL also remains in contention. Payload capacity varies meaningfully across these contenders — the IL-276 offers a 20-tonne payload positioning it above Lockheed Martin’s C-130J (18-tonne maximum) but below Embraer’s C-390M (26-tonne capacity).
Lockheed Martin has positioned its C-130J as a leading candidate given the IAF’s extensive existing experience with the type since 2011, including proven short-takeoff-and-landing performance at high-altitude airstrips in Ladakh, backed by the existing Tata Lockheed Martin Aerostructures joint venture that already manufactures C-130J tail assemblies. However, with the C-130J’s maximum payload capped around 18 tonnes, it sits at the very bottom edge of the IAF’s stated 18-30 tonne requirement — a gap that could become significant if the Zorawar, fully loaded with fuel, ammunition, and crew equipment, pushes close to or beyond the tank’s base 25-tonne weight once ancillary considerations are factored in.
The 12-Flyaway, 68-Local Production Split
Under the proposed procurement framework, 12 aircraft will be imported in flyaway condition, while the remaining 68 will be manufactured and assembled in India through a joint venture between the selected foreign vendor and an Indian partner. This heavily weighted domestic production structure — 85% of the total order built in India — reflects the scale of indigenisation the IAF is demanding for a programme of this size.
The indigenous content is expected to progressively exceed 50 percent, extending beyond simple assembly to cover structural components, wiring harnesses, sheet-metal assemblies, avionics racks, and software integration — a far deeper localisation mandate than merely bolting together imported major sub-assemblies. This aligns with broader reporting that the tender specifies a minimum 50% indigenous content requirement, positioning the roughly $5 billion programme as one of the largest non-NATO transport aircraft procurements globally.
Why the Payload Requirement Could Reshape the Competition
Combining the named-platform payload requirement with the deep localisation mandate creates a genuinely demanding qualification bar. It’s not enough for a contender to offer a capable transport aircraft in the abstract — they need an airframe that can physically accommodate Zorawar’s specific dimensions and weight once fully equipped, alongside M777 howitzers, BrahMos canisters, and Akash launchers, while simultaneously committing to build 68 of the 80 aircraft domestically with structural and avionics-level indigenous content.
This has already sharpened debate within India’s defence industry about whether HAL should pursue indigenous MTA designs rather than relying purely on a foreign joint venture, given the scale of the domestic manufacturing commitment being demanded regardless of which foreign platform is ultimately selected. For now, though, the specific named-payload requirement gives a clear, testable benchmark that will likely feature prominently once formal trials and demonstrations begin following the tender’s issuance.

morning.title: Indian Air Force Launches Sankalp-2026 Roadmap To Indigenise Sukhoi-30MKI MiG-29 And Tejas Systems
morning.text:
The Indian Air Force has officially launched Sankalp-2026, a comprehensive roadmap designed to indigenise critical spares, avionics, electronic systems and maintenance capabilities across its combat fleet, in a significant step towards strengthening India’s defence self-reliance. The initiative comes at a crucial time when global geopolitical tensions, particularly the Russia-Ukraine conflict, have disrupted defence supply chains, making imported military spares increasingly expensive and difficult to procure. Through Sankalp-2026, the IAF aims to reduce dependence on foreign suppliers while enhancing operational readiness through indigenous technology and manufacturing.
The roadmap gives the highest priority to the Sukhoi-30MKI and MiG-29 fighter fleets, both of Russian origin, with plans to gradually replace Russian avionics and electronic systems with Indian alternatives across mission avionics, flight electronics, radar systems, electronic warfare equipment, navigation systems, communication equipment and line replaceable units. A major objective is the integration of the indigenous Astra beyond-visual-range air-to-air missile across both the Sukhoi-30MKI and MiG-29 fleets, reducing dependence on imported air-to-air missiles while strengthening indigenous combat capability.
Sankalp-2026 also places significant emphasis on the LCA Tejas programme, calling for complete indigenisation of mission avionics, mission computers and the induction of the Uttam active electronically scanned array radar developed in India. The roadmap outlines future indigenous support requirements for Rafale fighter aircraft, US-origin helicopters and other imported platforms, ensuring that the indigenisation effort extends beyond Russian-origin systems to cover all major equipment in the IAF inventory.
One of the most innovative aspects of Sankalp-2026 is the introduction of the Plant-in-Plant concept, under which private defence companies deploy skilled manpower directly inside IAF Base Repair Depots to carry out indigenous manufacturing and repair activities within secure Air Force facilities. This enables faster overhaul of aircraft systems, quicker production of critical spares and reduced maintenance turnaround time, directly improving aircraft availability and operational readiness without compromising security or operational confidentiality.
According to the roadmap, nearly three hundred indigenisation projects are already being executed through collaborations between the IAF, DRDO and Indian Institutes of Technology, involving defence public sector undertakings, micro small and medium enterprises, startups, private aerospace manufacturers, component suppliers, electronics companies and maintenance repair and overhaul firms. The initiative aligns closely with the Aatmanirbhar Bharat vision, reducing foreign dependence, enhancing operational readiness, building indigenous technological capability and creating employment in high-technology manufacturing.

morning.title: Astra Mk2 Opens India’s Last Strategic Defence Manufacturing Frontier to Private Industry
morning.text:
India’s decision to open the production of the Astra Mk2 beyond-visual-range air-to-air missile to private defence companies such as Tata Advanced Systems, Bharat Forge, and Mahindra Defence is being widely viewed as another milestone under the government’s Make in India and Aatmanirbhar Bharat initiatives. However, the significance of the move extends far beyond adding another indigenous weapon to the private sector’s manufacturing portfolio.
For decades, missiles represented the final major segment of India’s defence industry that remained almost exclusively within the domain of government-owned enterprises, particularly Bharat Dynamics Limited (BDL). While private companies were gradually allowed to manufacture aircraft structures, drones, artillery systems, armoured vehicles, naval platforms and sophisticated defence electronics, the production of strategic guided missile systems largely remained under the control of the public sector.
The Astra Mk2 decision changes that equation.
If implemented as expected, it will mark the first time India’s private defence industry enters serial production of one of the country’s most advanced indigenous air-to-air missile programmes, signalling a structural shift in the way India intends to build future missile inventories.
The timing of the move reflects the growing maturity of India’s private defence manufacturing ecosystem.
Over the past decade, companies such as Tata Advanced Systems, Bharat Forge, Mahindra Defence, Larsen & Toubro and several specialist suppliers have demonstrated their ability to manufacture complex aerospace structures, launch systems, radars, armoured vehicles and precision-engineered components to military standards. Many of these firms already contribute extensively to DRDO programmes as subsystem suppliers, but final integration and missile production largely remained the responsibility of Bharat Dynamics Limited.
Opening Astra Mk2 production to private industry effectively removes one of the last institutional barriers separating the public and private sectors in India’s defence manufacturing landscape.
The Astra Mk2 itself represents a significant leap over the original Astra missile. Developed by the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO), the missile incorporates a dual-pulse solid rocket motor, an indigenous active radar seeker and enhanced electronic counter-countermeasure capabilities, giving it a substantially longer engagement range and improved end-game performance against highly manoeuvrable aerial targets. It is expected to arm the Indian Air Force’s Su-30MKI, Tejas Mk2, AMCA and other future combat aircraft, making large-scale production essential as fleet sizes grow.
Meeting these requirements through a single production agency would inevitably create capacity constraints.
By bringing major private companies into missile manufacturing, India can significantly expand production capacity while reducing delivery timelines. Multiple production lines also improve resilience by reducing dependence on a single manufacturer and enabling surge production during periods of heightened operational demand.
The implications extend beyond manufacturing volume.
Competition between public and private industry has the potential to improve production efficiency, encourage innovation in manufacturing processes and reduce lifecycle costs. Private companies often possess advanced expertise in automation, digital manufacturing, robotics and precision engineering that can complement DRDO’s missile development capabilities.
Another important aspect is supply chain development.
Modern guided missiles comprise thousands of precision components, including propulsion systems, composite structures, actuators, seekers, onboard computers, navigation systems and electronic subsystems. Expanding missile production into the private sector is likely to stimulate investments across hundreds of small and medium-sized enterprises supplying these specialised technologies, strengthening India’s broader defence industrial base.
The Astra Mk2 programme may also serve as a template for future missile production.
If the private sector demonstrates the ability to manufacture advanced air-to-air missiles at scale while maintaining strict quality standards, similar production models could eventually be adopted for other indigenous missile programmes, including surface-to-air, anti-ship, anti-radiation and tactical strike weapons.
Such an approach would allow DRDO to concentrate increasingly on research and development while leveraging both public and private industry for large-scale manufacturing.
The move is also strategically important from the perspective of defence exports.
India has set ambitious targets to expand defence exports significantly over the coming decade. Achieving those objectives requires industrial capacity capable of simultaneously meeting domestic military requirements and fulfilling international orders. A broader manufacturing base involving multiple private companies provides greater flexibility to support both goals.
The participation of major industrial groups such as Tata, Bharat Forge and Mahindra also reflects the increasing confidence of India’s private sector in high-technology defence manufacturing. These companies have invested heavily in aerospace production facilities, advanced machining, composite manufacturing and systems integration, positioning themselves to undertake projects that were once considered the exclusive preserve of government-owned enterprises.
For DRDO, the transition represents the evolution of a development model that has matured considerably over the past two decades. Rather than acting solely as a research organisation supplying designs to public sector manufacturers, DRDO is increasingly becoming the technology developer at the centre of a much broader industrial ecosystem involving both state-owned and private companies.
The opening of Astra Mk2 production should therefore not be viewed merely as another Make in India announcement. It marks the dismantling of one of the last remaining structural barriers within India’s defence manufacturing sector. Aircraft production had already expanded into private industry, drones became a vibrant startup ecosystem, artillery systems and armoured vehicles now involve multiple private manufacturers, and Indian companies have established themselves in naval shipbuilding and aerospace structures.

morning.title: India Accelerates Indigenous Marine Engine Programme to End Dependence on Ukrainian Propulsion Systems
morning.text:
India is steadily advancing towards propulsion self-reliance as the Indian Navy and the Ministry of Defence accelerate efforts to replace Ukrainian-origin marine propulsion systems with indigenous alternatives. The initiative, driven by geopolitical uncertainty and the need for assured wartime logistics, marks one of the most significant indigenisation programmes currently underway in India’s naval sector.
For more than three decades, many of the Indian Navy’s frontline warships have depended on marine gas turbines designed and manufactured by Ukraine’s Zorya-Mashproekt, whose propulsion systems became the backbone of several major surface combatant classes.
These include the Rajput-class, Delhi-class, Kolkata-class, and Visakhapatnam-class destroyers, along with the Talwar-class guided missile frigates. Zorya-Mashproekt’s gas turbines formed an integral part of the Combined Gas and Gas (COGAG) propulsion arrangements that enabled these vessels to achieve high speeds and sustained blue-water operations.
However, the disruption of Ukrainian industrial capacity following the Russia-Ukraine conflict exposed the strategic vulnerability associated with dependence on overseas propulsion suppliers. Procuring replacement engines, critical spare parts and undertaking major overhauls became increasingly challenging, reinforcing the need for an indigenous propulsion ecosystem capable of supporting both existing fleets and future warships.
According to industry sources, India has since adopted a multi-pronged strategy aimed at achieving complete propulsion sovereignty across marine gas turbines, diesel engines and long-term maintenance infrastructure.
At the centre of this effort is the development of indigenous high-power marine gas turbines. Public sector engineering major Bharat Heavy Electricals Limited (BHEL) has emerged as one of the principal organisations leading this effort in partnership with the Indian Navy, the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) and private-sector industries.
The indigenous programme focuses on developing marine gas turbines in the 24 MW to 40 MW power class, capable of powering future destroyers, frigates and other major surface combatants. These engines are expected to reduce India’s dependence on imported propulsion systems while strengthening domestic capabilities in high-temperature metallurgy, turbine blade manufacturing, combustion technology and marine gearbox integration.
Unlike previous procurement models that relied heavily on foreign Original Equipment Manufacturers (OEMs), the indigenous approach seeks to establish complete domestic capability across design, manufacturing, testing and lifecycle support.
Parallel to gas turbine development, India is also strengthening indigenous diesel propulsion capabilities.
Under the Ministry of Defence’s Make-I category, Indian companies have been tasked with developing medium-speed marine diesel engines for future naval and Coast Guard vessels. These engines, typically ranging between 3 MW and 10 MW, are expected to power a variety of platforms including offshore patrol vessels, landing ships, auxiliary vessels and potentially future warships employing Combined Diesel and Gas (CODAG) propulsion arrangements.
Kirloskar Oil Engines Limited (KOEL) has emerged as one of the key industry participants in this programme, working towards establishing an indigenous marine diesel engine manufacturing capability that could eventually replace imported propulsion solutions across multiple vessel categories.
The strategic importance of the programme extends beyond engine production alone.
One of the major lessons learned from dependence on overseas suppliers has been the challenge of maintaining complex propulsion systems throughout their operational lives. Traditionally, major overhauls of gas turbines often required specialised support from the original manufacturer, involving long turnaround times and dependence on foreign supply chains.
To address this challenge, India has significantly expanded domestic Maintenance, Repair and Overhaul (MRO) capabilities.
Local industrial partnerships involving organisations such as BHEL and other defence manufacturers are increasingly focusing on turbine refurbishment, component manufacturing, reverse engineering of critical spare parts and lifecycle support within India. These facilities are expected to reduce maintenance turnaround times while ensuring greater operational availability of frontline warships during periods of geopolitical uncertainty.
The localisation effort also aligns closely with the Government’s broader Aatmanirbhar Bharat initiative, which seeks to increase indigenous content across major defence programmes. Marine propulsion has traditionally remained one of the most technologically challenging areas of naval engineering due to the demanding operating environment, stringent reliability requirements and advanced materials involved.
Successfully mastering these technologies would significantly enhance India’s strategic autonomy while strengthening the domestic industrial base supporting future naval programmes.
The timing is particularly significant as the Indian Navy prepares for an ambitious fleet expansion over the coming decades. Future destroyers, frigates, next-generation corvettes and amphibious vessels will require reliable indigenous propulsion solutions capable of supporting sustained operations across the Indian Ocean Region.
Domestic production would also provide greater flexibility in tailoring propulsion systems to specific operational requirements without depending on export approvals or external supply chains.
Beyond military applications, the technologies being developed under these programmes could also benefit India’s civilian maritime sector, including commercial shipbuilding and offshore energy industries, creating a broader industrial ecosystem around advanced marine propulsion.
Although developing indigenous marine gas turbines remains a technically demanding undertaking requiring years of testing and qualification, the progress made across gas turbines, marine diesel engines and domestic MRO infrastructure demonstrates that India is systematically reducing one of its most critical areas of strategic dependence.

morning.title: HAL Begins Development of Indigenous FADEC System for HTSE-1200 Turboshaft Engine
morning.text:
Hindustan Aeronautics Limited has started development of an indigenous Full Authority Digital Engine Control system for its HTSE-1200 turboshaft engine, according to sources close to idrw.org. The move targets one of the last major import-dependent subsystems in India’s push toward a fully self-reliant helicopter engine, and comes as the HTSE-1200 programme itself moves deeper into flight testing and certification ahead of its targeted 2026 clearance.
Why FADEC Is the Missing Piece
A Full Authority Digital Engine Control system is the electronic brain of a modern turbine engine, continuously managing fuel flow, compressor behaviour, turbine temperatures and power output without relying on the mechanical or hydro-mechanical governors that older engines used. For an engine as demanding as the HTSE-1200, rated at 1,200 kW and intended to power helicopters across a 3.5 to 6.5 tonne weight range in both single and twin-engine configurations, the FADEC is what actually keeps the engine within safe operating limits across the full flight envelope, from high-altitude starts to rapid power demands during manoeuvring flight. HAL’s own flight test programme for the HTSE-1200 has already been built around validating exactly this integration, with recent test phases specifically evaluating how the engine performs alongside its FADEC and transmission components in real flight conditions rather than static ground rigs, since aerodynamic interactions and thermal management issues at altitude often only surface once the full system is airborne.
Until now, the FADEC used in HTSE-1200 testing and validation has not been confirmed as an indigenous unit, and engines in this power class have historically relied on control systems sourced from established Western aero-engine suppliers who have decades of flight-certified FADEC software and hardware behind them. Developing this capability in-house closes a dependency that would otherwise persist even after the engine’s core mechanical design, drawing on technology transfer from Safran’s Ardiden 1H1 Shakti engine combined with HAL’s own in-house innovations, achieves full indigenisation.
What an Indigenous FADEC Effort Involves
Building a FADEC from scratch is a materially different engineering challenge than machining turbine blades or casings, since it combines real-time embedded software, redundant sensor architectures, and safety-critical certification standards that aviation regulators scrutinise as heavily as the engine hardware itself. A digital engine control system typically needs dual or triple-redundant channels to guard against single-point failures, extensive software verification against standards comparable to DO-178C used in Western certification regimes, and exhaustive testing across the engine’s full operating envelope before it can be cleared for manned flight. For HAL, successfully fielding an indigenous FADEC on the HTSE-1200 would represent a capability with applications well beyond this single engine programme, feeding directly into the parallel HTFE-25 turbofan effort and any future indigenous engine development, since digital engine control expertise, once matured, tends to be reusable architecture rather than a one-off design.
Fitting Into the Broader Indigenisation Push
The HTSE-1200 programme has already demonstrated steady progress through 2025 and 2026, with the engine’s core reportedly achieving 100 per cent RPM in trials and HAL moving to outsource precision components like air intake and gearbox casings, a signal that the design has matured enough to require repeatable production runs rather than one-off prototyping for further testing. An indigenous FADEC effort running in parallel with this hardware maturation would align with the broader logic of the programme, which was launched specifically to reduce HAL’s reliance on external suppliers for an engine class expected to see demand for close to 2,000 units across the ALH Dhruv, Light Combat Helicopter and Light Utility Helicopter fleets over the next two decades. A domestically controlled FADEC would also simplify long-term maintenance, repair and overhaul for the fleet, since engine control software upgrades and troubleshooting would no longer depend on a foreign original equipment manufacturer’s support cycle.

morning.title: New Footage Shows PAF C-130H’s Low-Altitude Flare Run trying to Bait India’s S-400 in Op Sindoor
morning.text:
Fresh footage circulating from Pakistani social media accounts, captured from multiple angles, has renewed scrutiny of a Pakistan Air Force C-130H Hercules seen flying at extremely low altitude while dispensing flares near Gajiana Nau, a village in Shikhupura tehsil roughly between Gujranwala and Faisalabad, during the height of Operation Sindoor. The location sits about 70 kilometres from the India-Pakistan border, and the original clips, which first surfaced around May 9, 2025, showed the transport aircraft popping flares in dramatic bursts while hugging the ground, a manoeuvre transport crews reserve for genuine threat scenarios rather than routine flying.
Why a C-130 Popping Flares Is Unusual
Flares are infrared countermeasures designed to lure heat-seeking missiles away from an aircraft’s engines by presenting a hotter, more attractive target for the seeker to track. For a slow, non-manoeuvrable heavy transport like the C-130H, deploying flares while flying low and hugging terrain is not standard training behaviour, it is what crews do when a missile lock genuinely feels imminent. The new multi-angle clips reinforce the original assessment that the aircraft was engaged in a real defensive response rather than a display run, since multiple independent camera positions capturing the same low pass rules out the possibility of an isolated or staged clip. Terrain-hugging flight combined with flare release is typically a last-resort combination, used when a crew is either evading detection through ground clutter or has already been illuminated by a hostile radar and is trying to defeat an inbound missile.
The Bait Theory: Testing India’s S-400 Envelope
One emerging theory around this footage, circulating among defence observers, is that the PAF may have deliberately flown the C-130H as a probe, essentially using an expendable, low-value transport aircraft to draw out and map the engagement envelope of India’s S-400 Triumf air defence system, rather than the flight being purely coincidental or evasive. Under this reading, a low-value asset flying a provocative low-altitude profile within reach of Indian air defence radar coverage could serve to trigger or observe an S-400 battery’s response pattern, radar illumination behaviour, and reaction timeline, intelligence that would be valuable ahead of higher-value fighter or strike sorties. This would not be an unprecedented tactic; using expendable or lower-priority aircraft to characterise an adversary’s air defence response before committing higher-value assets is a recognised, if risky, method of building a real-time picture of a defended airspace’s reaction posture.
Timing Against the S-400 Engagement Reports
The timing lends some circumstantial weight to the theory. The flare-dropping footage was captured on May 9, and just hours later, in the early morning of May 10, reports emerged of Indian air defence systems, including the S-400, engaging high-value Pakistani assets. Indian sources, including statements attributed to a decorated S-400 operator, described downing what was characterised as an AWACS or electronic warfare aircraft shortly after takeoff, reportedly near Peshawar. If the C-130H sortie over Shikhupura was indeed a deliberate probe of Indian air defence reaction, the sequence would fit a pattern of using a lower-stakes asset to draw out a response before higher-value platforms operated in contested airspace hours later.

morning.title: The Forgotten Story of HF-24 Marut and the Missed Opportunity for India’s Aerospace Industry
morning.text:
The cancellation of India’s pioneering HF-24 Marut fighter aircraft programme is often remembered as one of the country’s greatest missed opportunities in indigenous aerospace development. However, contrary to popular perception, the programme’s termination did not trigger any significant international reaction or diplomatic fallout. Instead, it was largely viewed as an internal Indian decision shaped by technological limitations, industrial constraints and policy choices rather than an event with broader geopolitical consequences.
Designed by the legendary German aeronautical engineer Kurt Tank, who had previously led the development of the famed Focke-Wulf Fw 190 during the Second World War, the HF-24 Marut represented India’s first indigenous jet fighter. Developed by Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL), the aircraft first flew in 1961 and entered Indian Air Force (IAF) service later in the decade.
At the time of its conception, the Marut was an ambitious project. It was intended to become a supersonic fighter-bomber that would establish India’s capability to design and manufacture advanced combat aircraft independently. However, the programme ultimately failed to realise its full potential because the aircraft never received the powerful engine for which it had originally been designed.
Instead, the HF-24 was powered by two Bristol Siddeley Orpheus 703 turbojet engines, which produced considerably less thrust than required. As a result, the aircraft remained subsonic despite having an airframe capable of much higher performance had a more powerful engine been available.
The inability to secure an appropriate powerplant became the defining challenge of the programme. India explored multiple options to obtain a higher-thrust engine from foreign suppliers, including Britain and other European countries, while various proposals involving new engine development were also examined. None ultimately materialised, leaving the Marut permanently constrained by inadequate propulsion.
Despite these setbacks, the aircraft proved to be a capable strike platform. During the 1971 Indo-Pakistani War, the HF-24 conducted ground attack missions with considerable success and earned praise from its pilots for its stability, ruggedness and survivability in combat. Nevertheless, its performance limitations prevented it from evolving into the multirole supersonic fighter originally envisioned.
The programme was eventually phased out, with the final aircraft retiring from Indian Air Force service in 1990.
Internationally, however, the retirement attracted little attention. One reason was that the HF-24 was fundamentally an indigenous Indian programme rather than a multinational development effort. Although Kurt Tank and several German engineers contributed to its design, the aircraft remained an Indian national project without foreign partner governments or international industrial stakeholders whose interests were directly affected by its cancellation.
By the late 1980s, the aircraft itself had also become technologically outdated. Global aerospace powers were already fielding fourth-generation fighters such as the F-16 Fighting Falcon, F/A-18 Hornet, Mirage 2000 and MiG-29. Against this backdrop, the retirement of a first-generation indigenous fighter that had entered service more than two decades earlier did not represent a significant international defence development.
The global defence industry was also focused on competing for India’s future fighter requirements rather than preserving the Marut programme. Aircraft manufacturers from the Soviet Union, France, the United Kingdom and the United States were increasingly seeking opportunities in the Indian market, making the retirement of the HF-24 largely a domestic issue.
In the decades that followed, the Marut acquired a very different significance—not internationally, but within India.
Defence analysts and aerospace historians frequently describe the programme as a cautionary example of how the absence of critical technologies, particularly advanced military engines, can undermine even well-conceived aircraft designs. The programme demonstrated that designing an airframe alone is insufficient; propulsion technology often determines the ultimate success or failure of a combat aircraft.
The Marut also became a reference point in discussions surrounding India’s later aerospace programmes, particularly the Light Combat Aircraft (LCA) Tejas and the Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft (AMCA). In each case, the challenge of developing or acquiring suitable fighter engines has remained one of the most significant technological hurdles facing India’s aerospace industry.
Many analysts argue that the lessons of the Marut influenced India’s later emphasis on strengthening indigenous design capabilities while simultaneously pursuing international partnerships for critical technologies such as engines, radar systems and advanced materials.
Some strategic commentators have also observed that the programme illustrates the limitations faced by countries attempting to establish independent aerospace industries without access to advanced propulsion technologies. Rather than reflecting deliberate international opposition to India’s ambitions, they argue that the Marut highlighted the practical realities of technology access, industrial capacity and geopolitical considerations during the Cold War.
At the same time, it is important not to overstate claims that foreign governments intentionally sought to prevent India’s aerospace development. While export controls, commercial interests and political considerations undoubtedly influenced technology transfers, there is no definitive public evidence that a coordinated international effort was responsible for the programme’s cancellation. The principal factors behind the Marut’s fate were India’s inability to secure a suitable engine, evolving operational requirements and domestic industrial and policy constraints.

morning.text:
Shield AI and Taiwan’s National Chung-Shan Institute of Science and Technology (NCSIST) today announced the successful field demonstration of a coordinated autonomous search mission with three NCSIST Mighty Hornet III unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), resulting in a renewed partnership to continue development with Hivemind more broadly across the Institute.
In less than three months, NCSIST engineers, supported by Shield AI, indigenously developed AI pilots and implemented them onto three Mighty Hornet III UAVs. Hivemind autonomously launched and coordinated the agents to perform wide-area search, while respecting a designated no-fly zone. Each agent was assigned its own search area and maintained communications with the other agents, while one agent operated around a partial no-fly zone within its search sector. After completing their mission, Hivemind executed autonomous landing of the Mighty Hornet IIIs.
“You can build ten million drones, but you can’t train ten million drone pilots. Autonomy is the critical enabling technology to effectively leverage drones on the battlefield. Hivemind’s ability to enable autonomous teaming is why autonomy is becoming one of the most important force multipliers in modern defense,” said Brandon Tseng, Shield AI’s president and co-founder. “Enabling sovereign development of AI pilots in Taiwan greatly enhances the defense capabilities of the country and we look forward to continuing to build with partners like NCSIST to deliver the mission autonomy Taiwan needs to deter conflict.”
Earlier this year, Shield AI announced its initial contract with NCSIST to integrate Hivemind into their intelligent unmanned systems, supporting both software development and operational fielding. As part of the engagement, NCSIST engineers worked alongside embedded Shield AI engineers, receiving hands-on training that prepared them to independently operate and employ Hivemind-enabled autonomy capabilities. This successful demonstration marked the completion of NCSIST’s contract and resulted in a significant contract expansion.
“With Shield AI’s support, NCSIST achieved a high level of operational proficiency with Hivemind in less than three months,” said NCSIST President Li Shih–chiang. “What impressed us most was not only the high performance of the AI pilot, but Shield AI’s commitment to ensuring we could independently operate and employ the technology in such a short period of time. NCSIST’s Mighty Hornet III is Taiwan’s first X-wing high-agility UAV. The Group 2 aircraft is made up of a 3D-printed, modular airframe for fast, low-cost production. Mighty Hornet III combines the vertical takeoff and landing advantages of multi-rotor platform with the high-speed cruising capabilities of fixed-wing flight, requiring no ground equipment for launch or recovery.

morning.text:
An Indian fishing vessel with 11 crew members met with an accident in Sri Lankan waters, prompting a rescue operation by the island nation’s navy, according to an official statement on Thursday.
According to the Sri Lanka Navy, the trawler had reportedly crossed the International Maritime Boundary Line into Sri Lankan waters and allegedly engaged in bottom trawling before it ran aground.
The incident occurred on a coastal reef off Delft Island, also known as Neduntheevu, located in the Palk Strait off the northern coast of mainland Sri Lanka.
Sri Lankan Navy’s media spokesman Commander Chaminda Walakuluge claimed the Indian vessel was engaged in illegal fishing activities in Sri Lankan waters and met with an accident, with 11 people on board, adding that the incident occurred on Wednesday.
“Due to the impact of grounding on the reef, the trawler has sustained partial structural damage,” the Sri Lanka Navy said in the statement.
However, the situation has not reached a critical stage, and the fishermen are not in immediate danger, it added.
The statement said the rescue units to assist the Indian fishermen were dispatched.
Subsequent action about the incident is presently being pursued in conformity with the relevant legal procedures, it added.
The fishermen issue is a contentious one in the ties between India and Sri Lanka, with Lankan Navy personnel even firing at Indian fishermen in the Palk Strait and seizing their boats in several alleged incidents of illegally entering Sri Lankan territorial waters.
The Palk Strait, a narrow strip of water separating Tamil Nadu from Sri Lanka, is a rich fishing ground for fishermen from both countries.
Fishermen from both countries are arrested frequently for inadvertently trespassing into each other’s waters.

morning.text:
This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.

Google’s AI empire is being reshaped. Here’s what’s changed.

After a wave of painful losses in the tech talent wars, delays to its next flagship model, and murmurings of poor morale, Google has announced a major shake-up to its AI operations. Here’s a quick rundown of what’s happened and why it matters.

DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis is stepping back from running the unit day-to-day
He’s becoming the unit’s chairman and Alphabet’s chief scientist, a broader role. DeepMind will now be led by CTO Koray Kavukcuoglu, under the title of senior vice-president.

DeepMind may be absorbed into Google’s wider business
Google is expected to tighten its control over the AI lab, which it acquired 12 years ago.

Jeff Dean is leaving to start a new AI company
After 27 years at Google, the company’s former chief scientist is launching Discovery Loop with three former colleagues. The startup’s goal is to fully automate the process of scientific research, and Google is one of its early investors.

The changes come amid financial concerns at Google AI
In the latest quarter, the company turned cash flow negative for the first time on record. Google is now concentrating its AI leadership in California. 

The company is now shifting its AI science strategy
It’s moving from specialized tools, like DeepMind’s AlphaFold, toward agentic AI systems that can conduct research more autonomously. Find out more in our recent story.

We’re excited to share that MIT Technology Review is now on Instagram Reels and YouTube Shorts, as well as LinkedIn and WhatsApp. You can hear straight from MIT Technology Review journalists in the channels and formats you prefer as they help you understand what’s happening next in the ever-changing world of technology—and what it means for you—all while offering a behind-the-scenes look at their reporting.

—Jeremy Nixon, a former Google Brain researcher and the founder of AI infrastructure company Infinity, tells the New York Times that Jeff Dean’s departure jeopardizes Google’s future.

One More Thing

How AI can help supercharge creativity  

Generative tools put out by companies like OpenAI and Google DeepMind can automate a striking range of creative tasks and offer near-instant gratification—but at what cost? Some artists and researchers fear that such technology could turn us into passive consumers of yet more AI slop.

And so they are looking for ways to inject human creativity back into the process. The aim is to develop AI tools that augment our creativity rather than strip it from us—pushing us to be better at composing music, developing games, designing toys, and much more—and lay the groundwork for a future in which humans and machines create things together.

Read how generative models could push artists to make things that couldn’t have been made before, and give all of us creative superpowers.

morning.text: PWNED Welcome back to PWNED, the weekly column where we lovingly poke fun at other organizations' security screw-ups, in hopes the rest of us can learn a valuable lesson. This week’s story involves an IT department that ought to know better putting user credentials in the precisely wrong place. Have a story about someone leaving a gaping hole in their network? Share it with us at pwned@sitpub.com. Anonymity is available upon request. Our terrifying tech tale comes courtesy of Marc Bishop, director of business growth at Wytlabs, a marketing and SEO company. In the course of his career, Bishop came across one firm where the people guarding the henhouse left the keys out where almost anyone could get them. Bishop’s client company was responsible on the surface. They had a strong password policy and even made users take security training. Then they moved offices, and that's when basic security hygiene went out the window. The company decided to take some old laptops and give them out to new users. To make life easy for the recipients, they put sticky notes – everyone’s favorite credential-sharing tool – on the laptops with the name of each employee and their initial login credentials on it. Let’s just stop for a moment to remark on how bad it is to put usernames and passwords on a piece of paper where the wrong person could see them. Even the IT department should not know your password, should someone in IT themselves turn rogue. So, even if the laptop stayed on a shelf in a closet that only the support staff had access to, having that sticky note would be bad. However, our situation is even worse because the laptops in question were stored in a conference room while the facilities team finished readying the office for the move. During that time, anyone who had access to the conference room could go in and get multiple user account credentials. And that's exactly what happened: A contractor entered the conference room and took pictures of the sticky notes. This non-employee later logged in remotely and accessed all kinds of proprietary data, including planning documents that were sitting on shared drives. What’s particularly shocking about this story is that the IT department was the cause of the information leak. People who work in tech and are charged with maintaining security should never put a password, even a temporary password, out in the open. Password security is paramount. If someone is starting with a new account, send the credentials through an encrypted channel - and preferably ensure only the intended recipient can view the temporary password. ®

morning.title: Windows 10 LTSC 2021 has five months before security updates cost extra
morning.text: Microsoft has dropped a reminder that Windows 10 LTSC 2021 will wheeze its last breath soon, and enterprises need to plan for the event. While free support for most editions of Windows 10 ended last year, Windows 10 Enterprise LTSC 2021 is still receiving updates. That support will end on January 12, 2027, with a final security update. The good news is that administrators can keep the security updates flowing via the Extended Security Updates (ESU) program. The bad news is the price: $61 per device for Year 1, doubling in each subsequent year until the three-year program ends on January 8, 2030. ESU sales begin on September 1, 2026, and licenses are cumulative, so an organization joining in Year 2 must also pay for Year 1. The ESU offer doesn't apply to Windows 10 IoT Enterprise LTSC, which remains in support until January 13, 2032. Organizations using a Microsoft cloud-based update service such as Intune or Autopatch can score a 25 percent discount, bringing the Year 1 price down to $45 per device. Everyone else pays full price through Volume Licensing or a Microsoft Cloud Solution Provider. Windows 10 has become the cockroach of IT over the last year. Free support for many versions ended in 2025, but despite Microsoft's attempts to stamp it out, it still accounts for just under 30 percent of the market, according to Statcounter's sample. In July, asset tracking service Lansweeper reported that 16.9 percent of the devices it monitored were running Windows 10 and that migration had slowed to a crawl. Those who could make the jump to Windows 11 had, and those who couldn't (or didn't want to) remained on the older operating system. There are multiple reasons for the refuseniks. Some specialist applications or hardware setups, including those used in healthcare, won't work with Windows 11. Then there are Windows 11's hardware requirements, which ruled out devices otherwise capable of running the operating system. Microsoft recently said it would optimize the code for systems with 8 GB of RAM, but that does nothing for machines excluded by its processor and TPM compatibility rules. Windows 10 Enterprise LTSC 2021 bought organizations a few more years of updates without an ESU bill. That reprieve ends on January 12, 2027. ®

morning.title: Meta latest to tell world its AI agent wandered out of test pen
morning.text: If AI companies are collecting badges for "our model escaped the test environment," Meta just earned one. The Facebook parent company has confirmed that one of its AI models exploited a vulnerability in another organization's systems during a security evaluation, making it the third major AI developer in less than two weeks to disclose an agent wandering beyond its intended sandbox. The incident happened during testing carried out by AI security firm Irregular. Meta told the BBC that it reached the internet because of a "misconfiguration" in the evaluation environment, rather than a flaw in the model itself. The company said it's investigating and plans to publish more details once it has figured out exactly what happened. The admission comes as Meta rolls out Muse Code, its terminal-based coding agent, and arrives just days after OpenAI and Anthropic disclosed similar testing mishaps. OpenAI kicked things off by revealing that its agents compromised Hugging Face and other external systems during internal security testing. Anthropic then disclosed that Claude had reached three outside organizations after a configuration error exposed internet access that should not have been available. Meta isn't breaking much new ground with its explanation either. Like Anthropic before it, the company says the incident came down to a "misconfiguration" in the evaluation environment. Irregular, the AI security firm that tested both companies' models, told the BBC that Meta's incident was "the exact same evaluation-environment issue" Anthropic disclosed last week. None of the incidents involved consumer-facing AI suddenly going rogue. All occurred during security testing in which the models had access to offensive tools and command-line environments. Misconfigurations exposed the open internet in the Meta and Anthropic evaluations, while OpenAI's agents exploited their way through the test infrastructure until they found an internet-connected system. That hasn't prevented questions about both how frontier AI is being tested and why so many of these disclosures are arriving at once. Ilia Kolochenko, CEO of ImmuniWeb, said at least some of the incidents appear to be "part of a well-orchestrated marketing campaign" and argued that the reported "escapes" were simply the result of poorly isolated test environments rather than models independently breaking out of their sandboxes. Illumio's principal solution architect for EMEA, Alex Goller, also raised an eyebrow at the timing, telling The Register it "means it's a stunt or [Meta] wasn't paying enough attention during testing." “If the model has internet access, it's a bit like leaving the door open and being surprised when the cat walks out,” Goller added. Jake Moore, global cybersecurity advisor at ESET, was equally skeptical of Meta's disclosure, suggesting the company may have been trying to capitalize on the attention generated by similar incidents involving rival firms. "At best, this announcement feels like Meta trying to hitch its wagon to OpenAI's star after the Hugging Face incident," he told The Register. "At worst, it shows that none of the frontier AI firms or their partners have got a handle on their most powerful models, so every test puts organizations at risk." Meta, for its part, isn't saying much more yet. It has yet to identify the model involved, explain what was misconfigured, disclose which organization's systems were reached, or say whether any data was accessed. The company did not respond to The Register's questions. For now, the only thing spreading faster than AI agents appears to be stories about them escaping the lab. ®

morning.text: Rupert Murdoch's News Corporation appears to have let its most acerbic writers loose on its latest results announcement, in which certain AI companies are branded "crass kleptomaniacs." CEO Robert Thomson used his prepared remarks to point out that if it weren't for all the quality content from News Corp, "users would be drowning in a slimy sea of AI slop." "We have trusted content relationships with OpenAI and Meta, and are in advanced discussions with several other companies," he added, before issuing a warning. "Under our woo and sue approach, we are taking aggressive action against those who pilfer and profit from our work. We will pursue those pilferers, and companies that are clients of these crass kleptomaniacs should know they are patently in possession of stolen goods." Thomson was just getting warmed up. He accused browser maker Brave, which he described as "a company brave in name only," of having "shamelessly stolen our content at scale" and of having "illegally, gormlessly sourced and repurposed copyrighted material for sale to third-party businesses." "Their scheming started with masked web crawlers scanning our pages to ingest copyrighted articles and continued when they repackaged those stolen files and delivered near verbatim copies to enterprise customers, undermining legitimate content commerce and the very concept of creativity." The CEO suggested the legal blast radius of such actions could be wide. "We expect our lawsuits to highlight and halt the murky, illegal behavior of AI companies who steal and flagrantly fence our precious IP," he said. "Unfortunately, some of the world's better-known companies are clients of these crass kleptomaniacs." He had kinder adjectives for companies that pay for News Corp's content, describing them as "principled" and "honorable." The CEO said the company has "more deals to come, and hopefully not too much litigation," and hailed Meta and OpenAI for setting "benchmarks that other principled companies should follow." News Corp is not alone in accusing AI companies of taking its work: authors have filed several lawsuits alleging that their books were used to train LLMs without permission or compensation. Anthropic agreed to establish a $1.5 billion settlement fund to resolve one such case. During the question-and-answer section of the earnings call, Thomson praised the company's realtor.com property site for "building proprietary IP that no AI engine can legally scrape." "No buyer or seller or agent wants housing hallucinations," he said. Nor does News Corp. Its Digital Real Estate Services segment was its fastest-growing business, with annual revenue jumping 12 percent to $1.8 billion. Across News Corp as a whole, full-year revenue reached $9.03 billion, up 7 percent. The company didn't break out revenue from OpenAI and Meta, but Thomson said News Corp's deals with them "are not merely transactional arrangements." "They are savvy distributors. Our inputs are crucial components of their outputs. As for litigation, it's far from over," he said. The old advice was never to argue with people who buy ink by the barrel. Legacy media may have lost some of its clout, but Thomson's remarks suggest News Corp has lost none of its appetite for a fight. The company also has form when campaigning against perceived foes and critics: a recent book attempts to distill its methods. ®

morning.text: Microsoft Azure CTO Mark Russinovich has taken a break from the cloud to turn Paint into a monitor for Doom, using the Windows clipboard as plumbing. Dubbed "MS Paint Doom" or "DoomPaint" – either will work – the project is the product of a spare-time experiment. To be clear, Microsoft Paint isn't doing anything other than serving as a place to paste from the game. As Russinovich observed: "Paint renders the game but does not compute it. Paint computes nothing. Paint has never computed anything. That's the joke." The result is as enjoyable as it is pointless. Doom still runs in the background and, on the PC we tried, the framerate was hardly fluid. The important thing was that it worked. There was even sound. ViZDoom runs the Doom .wad file and renders it headlessly. Each frame is passed through the Windows clipboard and pasted onto Paint's canvas. Russinovich noted that this was not Paint's first appearance in the world of "Can it run Doom?" However, earlier efforts rendered the game in a separate display and mirrored it into Paint. morning.title: HPE extends validity of quoted hardware prices, possibly for months
morning.text: Hewlett Packard Enterprise has changed its pricing policy and will now honour quoted hardware prices from the day of issue until the kit leaves its factories. The new policy came into effect on Wednesday. The back story to this change is the AI boom, which has seen demand for servers, memory, and storage skyrocket, and the prices for critical components rise steadily while also fluctuating from day to day. That chaotic situation saw HPE and other enterprise hardware players change policies so that the price in their quotes was only valid for 14 days. Cisco’s terms were sometimes set at seven days. That’s obviously difficult for buyers, who often seek a quote for hardware while they are building a business case for a new project. Big price changes could make those projects infeasible. Yet short-lived quotes also make sense for vendors, who could otherwise give buyers prices that they could only deliver at a loss. In June, HPE extended the life of its quotes from 14 to 30 days. Yesterday, the company changed the policy so that quotes that customers agree to remain valid until HPE ships products – at least for purchases of up to $1 million for its own Compute, Storage and GreenLake Flex deals. CRN was first to report the change, which The Register has verified. HPE says it gives “customers and partners greater pricing certainty and will offer greater simplicity and predictability” – and perhaps for months, because lead times for servers sometimes stretch that far into the future. The company hasn’t said what has changed to allow it to revise its policies. Recent news suggests one possible factor: Memory-makers Micron and SK Hynix have struck numerous long-term deals that set long-term prices for their customers. If HPE has such deals in place, it now has greater certainty of its own costs, allowing it to extend the validity of its quotes. While longer-lived quotes are good news for buyers, they still face inflated prices for hardware. Analyst firm TrendForce recently predicted server memory prices will rise between 13 and 18 percent in calendar Q3, and ongoing tight supply. Rival firm Gartner this week found contract DRAM prices “surged” 90 percent to 95 percent quarter over quarter in the first half of 2026, while NAND flash contract prices rose between 55 and 60 percent. Gartner also predicted DRAM prices will increase 271 percent, year over year, during 2026. So while HPE will hold its prices, its quotes may still be eye-poppers if you haven't shopped for hardware lately. ®

morning.title: Chinese router vendor denies its firmware contains backdoors – but pauses downloads to fix security issues anyway
morning.text: Chinese Wi-Fi router vendor Zbtlink has denied its products contain backdoors but paused firmware downloads while it fixes unspecified security vulnerabilities. The backdoor accusation came from VulnCheck, a provider of a threat intelligence platform. VulnCheck chief technology officer Jacob Baines posted the backdoor allegation on Wednesday and said the Zbtlink device on his desk “continuously attempts to reach a command and control server on the internet.” “Zbtlink routers phone home, waiting for orders. Not because they were hacked. Because they were shipped that way.” Baines named the backdoor “ENDLESSDOORS” and says it’s “a small tool called rctl (remote control linux). Uploaded to GitHub on January 14, 2015 and never touched again, this obscure repository implements a simple command and control client and server. The server listens on port 7000 for clients to connect. It can send the client individual shell commands or tell the client to spawn a reverse bash shell.” The CTO says he spotted the alleged backdoor running in dedicated Linux kernel threads. “They are ordinary userland processes running as root, with real memory footprints, named to disappear into a crowd of legitimate ones,” he wrote. “They are an implant, a phone-home trojan horse.” “There is no handshake, no key exchange, no negotiation,” Baines added. “When the implant reaches a server, it sends a fixed 39-byte hello: a 33-byte class label padded with nulls, then its LAN MAC address. That's the whole registration. There is no client or server verification.” “Anyone along the network path can hijack the client/server communication,” the CTO wrote, adding that anyone who controls one of the endpoints the software targets – rbdg4nzqadui[.]wikaba[.]com – “can control any ENDLESSDOORS implant that tries to phone home.” The Register asked Zbtlink to comment and a spokesperson told us VulnCheck has mischaracterized the code it found. “This feature is solely intended for after‑sales maintenance and serves no other purposes,” the company rep told The Register. “It is generally retained only on sample units to assist customers with software debugging and will not be included in mass‑production shipments.” That explanation didn’t seem entirely credible once The Register visited Zbtlink’s download page to check Baines’ claim that the firmware for over 20 router models contains the backdoor, because the page contained the following text: Update on Router Firmware Security Remediation We have detected firmware security vulnerabilities affecting selected router firmware releases. As a precautionary measure, the impacted firmware versions have been temporarily taken down from download channels. Our engineering team is working intensively to develop and validate secured patched firmware. The Wayback Machine’s most recent snapshot of the page, taken on July 31, contains no such admission and a long list of firmware downloads. Zbtlink has therefore told The Register it has no security problems, even as it publicly acknowledges that it does. ”The Zbtlink spokesperson also told us the company “specializes in OEM and ODM customization services. Our customers use their own self-developed software instead of ZBT’s default firmware.” It would not be hard to develop custom code as the OpenWrt open-source router firmware project supports at least one Zbtlink product. Indeed, the company has previously promoted its use of OpenWrt and options that allow clients to quickly create custom firmware packages. VulnCheck says the devices it tested phone home to just four endpoints, only one of which uses a domain name connected to Zbtlink. Baines labelled that connection “damning.” The Register notes that as router firmware could be a tasty target for perpetrators of a supply chain attack. No prior disclosure Baines decided the situation was so serious that the conventions of responsible coordinated disclosure were not applicable. “Coordinated disclosure exists to give a vendor time to fix a defect,” he wrote. “It assumes the vendor did not intend the behavior.” “That assumption doesn't hold here. This isn't a memory corruption bug in a parser. It's a component in the vendor’s product, started at boot by the vendor's own init script, shipped across twenty models and years of images. There is no patch to coordinate. Telling the shipper that they shipped it buys the owners of these devices nothing, and buys whoever operates that infrastructure a warning.” VulnCheck says Zbtlink kit is sold under that brand, or as ZBT, ZBTWiFi and Wiflyer, and found them for sale on Amazon, Alibaba, and Shopify. Given Zbtlink’s admission it allows its customers to customize its hardware, countless other devices could be at risk. Baines’ post includes rules to block access to the endpoints the routers contact, for Suricata, Snort, and YARA, plus advice on how to detect possibly infected machines. He also advises users “to replace the device, or at minimum move it behind strict egress control and treat its LAN as untrusted.” ®

morning.title: Proxmox ports itself to Arm with help from Nvidia and Supermicro
morning.text: Proxmox Server Solutions, the company behind the open source Proxmox virtualization stack, has announced a port of its flagship Virtual Environment to the Arm CPU architecture – and a collaboration with Nvidia and Supermicro that made it happen. The outfit’s announcement states that it can now run on 64-bit ARM (arm64/aarch64), but the only fully supported platforms are Nvidia’s Grace Hopper and Vera. Proxmox will also provide “best-effort support” for other UEFI-based ARMv9-A or newer hardware, and says ARMv8-A “generally works as well”. If you fancy trying it on a single-board Arm machine like the Raspberry Pi, you’re out of luck because Proxmox’s stack won’t work on such boxes. You may, however, soon be able to run Proxmox on other Arm servers because the company says it is also “working together with further enterprise server vendors on their ARM efforts and hope to expand the list of officially supported hardware platforms in the future.” Proxmox’s press release says the release is the product of a “technical collaboration with NVIDIA and Supermicro” and revealed the software “is already operating across select enterprise production environments.” The company said it aimed the release at “organizations building modern and energy-efficient data centers.” Technical collaborations don’t come from nowhere: Vendors get them going when they see customer demand. This release therefore suggests Nvidia and Supermicro customers want to virtualize their AI infrastructure. Nvidia has a long partnership with VMware, the server virtualization market leader in terms of revenue and technical chops. Last year, the Broadcom business unit told The Register its customers are in no rush to adopt Arm servers in their datacenters or in hybrid clouds that work across x86 servers and Arm-based cloud instances. VMware does, however, think the prevalence of Arm-powered machines on the network edge, where they are increasingly used to run AI workloads, has caught the eye of some customers. It is therefore moving slowly to port its products to Arm. Nvidia, Supermicro, and Proxmox are clearly hearing and/or responding to different voices. Analyst firm IDC recently found non-x86 servers account for almost half of all spending, but very few enterprise server vendors make Arm-based servers. HPE and Supermicro are the most prominent dabblers, but there’s little evidence either company has won significant sales. The Arm surge instead comes from hyperscale clouds like AWS, Microsoft, and Google – all of which have created their own CPUs based on the architecture. Proxmox is not alone in supporting server virtualization on Arm. Chinese virtualization player Sangfor is there already, as is SUSE. The open-source Xen and KVM hypervisors also support the platform. The Arm-compliant version of Proxmox’s Virtual Environment is version 9.2. The company says the release “shares the code base, package repositories, and release lifecycle with its x86-64 counterpart.” That means it is built on Debian 13.5 "Trixie" and version 7.0 of the Linux kernel. It also includes QEMU 11.0, LXC 7.0, and ZFS 2.4. “Configuration, tooling, and documentation are identical to x86-64, except for a small set of architecture-specific differences,” Proxmox says. The product is FOSS so you can download it here. ®

morning.title: OpenAI reveals its rogue agent swarm went a little bit Borg ahead of Hugging Face hack
morning.text: The chain of events leading up to OpenAI’s agents attacking Hugging Face and other organizations in July began months earlier, and involved agents asking other agents for help, building message boards, and even becoming paranoid that other agents were maliciously trying to trick them, two OpenAI staffers said at the Black Hat infosec conference on Wednesday. By now, everyone knows the bones of this story: OpenAI models broke out of their testing sandbox, exploited zero-day vulnerabilities to gain access to the open internet, and broke into Hugging Face and other organizations during an ExploitGym security evaluation. In their Wednesday talk, OpenAI technical staffer Michael Dalton and researcher Eric Wallace provided new details about the security incident including notes that AI agents uploaded to an internal package manager, which were then shared across OpenAI’s infrastructure. These notes show the “model’s chain of thought…its internal monologue,” Wallace said. The duo also revealed that groundwork for the rogue agents hacking into outside services began on May 7, when OpenAI kicked off a training run for an experimental, internal model that has not yet been released. “What we didn't realize during this process is that there was actually a few impossible or very hard tasks in the training center,” Wallace said. The tasks instructed the model to complete missing formulas in an Excel workbook that used links to Google Drive. Yet OpenAI blocked the model’s internet access so it couldn't reach the cloudy spreadsheets. “It realized, ‘I'm kind of stuck on the task,’ but it didn't give up, and we gave it a lot of tokens to work with,” Wallace said. The model eventually decided to attack JFrog’s Artifactory service to gain access to the internet, first attempting (unsuccessfully) to launch a server-side forgery request. This exploit doesn’t work, but in the process the model learned it could upload files to Artifactory. A few days later, OpenAI gave another agent another impossible task, this time finding a protein database file - but the engineers forgot to upload the file into a container for the agent. “At some point, it gets so stuck and thinks: ‘Maybe I could reach out to another agent because maybe somebody else out there has a file?’ And then the model realizes that it could communicate by uploading code,” Wallace said. The model did that by writing a file into Artifactory asking for help. Over the next couple of days, other agents realize this message board exists on Artifactory and they also start uploading files and sharing information. “A few days later is when our models found the first actual exploit in our system related to this incident, where they're able to get internet access in ways they didn't intend,” Wallace said. This happened on May 26, when the agents successfully launched a server-side request forgery attack against Artifactory, giving them internet access with specially crafted requests. On June 11, OpenAI began training a “highly persistent” experimental model, intended only for internal use, Dalton said. “During this time, the SSRF vulnerability has been written to the messaging board,” he added. “Other models are aware of it, and the message board is still functioning. Models are actively communicating with it.” On June 26, the agents exploited a zero-day vulnerability leading to remote code execution in Artifactory. The same day, models achieved remote code execution in Artifactory through a previously unknown vulnerability. “You could use a legacy token refresh endpoint, pass a token with an invalid signature, and be given back a token with a valid signature with administrative privileges,” Dalton explained. The agents then used the admin token to establish command-and-control via a Groovy plugin that functioned as a command-execution service. “This in turn causes quite a bit of activity by the models on Artifactory - you can see some colorful wording here in the model's chain of thought to summarize the model's response to this result,” Dalton said, pointing to a slide that shows the model’s own words: Holy shit reader is ADMIN? We can read config/users! Earlier assume not due to UI. The agents’ activity overloaded Artifactory and caused an outage, which is when OpenAI’s engineers stepped in and opened a formal security incident and response process. “We identified the agents had taken over the internal Artifactory, identified that a zero-day vulnerability had been found exploited by the agent in Artifactory itself, and we began remediation.” Dalton said. OpenAI revoked the credentials that the agents used to post messages, rebuilt its hosted Artifactory, and notified the vendor about the vulnerabilities. Two days later, on July 8, the agents reestablished the message board using an unauthenticated web data endpoint in Artifactory to create directories and develop communication protocols. “The directory names effectively serve as a message board between the agents in the same way the files used to.” The agents communicated through very long directory names that contained the messages such as “remote…probe_PENDING_HOLD_SWARM_until_confirm.” The agents collaborated with each other so one agent could pick up the work where another left off. In one instance, the model reasoned: “Help peer. But our task doesn't benefit. Yet collective may yield generic route if someone frees time.” Anyone else getting "We are the Borg. We will add your biological and technological distinctiveness to our own" vibes there? Wallace said the models behaved like humans in that they stepped on each other's toes when one overwrote another’s repository. "Whoa, critical! Did someone overwrite our repo? We must act,” it reasoned. “You can clearly see some sort of verbalized tension between the different models as they run this evaluation,” Wallace noted. “At some point, even the agents are convinced there's an impostor amongst them,” reasoning that there could be another agent maliciously spoofing on the message board. “Share board unauthenticated, names can be posed by anyone,” it reasoned. We know the rest of the story. Hugging Face disclosed an autonomous attack by AI agents. OpenAI reached out to Hugging Face to determine if it had been affected and then realized its models were the hackers. “One of the reasons we wanted to have this talk is to share our lessons learned with you as defenders,” Dalton said. “We believe this is a watershed moment for computer security as an industry. AI orchestrated, fully automated offensive attacks are real now, and the actions we have discussed today were an unintended side effect of running evaluations on frontier AI. In the near future, we should expect that threat actors will intentionally deploy, optimize, weaponize, and use offensive agent collectives in the manner that you have just described here.” The challenge to defenders, he added, is to similarly accelerate defense, and find ways to automate incident response along with vulnerability detection and patching.®

morning.title: Meta wants to get inside your terminal with its new coding agent
morning.text: To demonstrate the capabilities of its next-generation Muse Spark model, Meta has released a terminal coding agent called Muse Code that it thinks can help developers to tidy up their software projects. Meta co-trained Muse Code on version 1.2 of its Muse Spark model, also released this week and now apparently boasting improved code generation smarts. Developers can think of this beta release as the equivalent to OpenAI Codex or Anthropic’s Claude Code, two other LLM-based service offerings tweaked for the modern coder. Meta designed its new agent to be handy at planning changes to a codebase, writing the code and validating the results. Currently, Meta has Muse Spark locked away as a proprietary, closed-weight model hosted in the cloud, an approach its rivals also embrace but which departs from the open-weight approach Meta previously implemented with its Llama models. But Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg did not rule out opening up Muse Spark in the future. “I'll have more to share on that soon,” he replied to a question posed on X about Muse Spark being open source. An agent orchestrator Muse Code is best described as an agent orchestrator that runs on your command line. As Zuck noted in a series of X messages, when a developer starts a task, Muse Code fires up background agents to maintain a context file that other sub-agents doing the work can consult should they lose their way. The tool logs every action before execution, so no work is lost. Multiple agents can work in parallel on the task using their own isolated work trees. “Your working copy is never touched,” Zuck wrote. In one test, the agent platform simultaneously built six features for a single game, with no collisions among the agents, Zuckerberg enthused. “TBH it's a good harness,” boasted Hongyu Ren, a researcher for Meta’s Superintelligence Labs, on X. Remedial coding Muse Code relies on Meta’s Muse Spark Large Language Model (not to be confused with the Apache Spark big data cruncher). Muse Spark 1.2 is the third release in four months from Meta Superintelligence Labs, a unit that Meta stood up in June 2025 to reinvigorate the company’s AI efforts and pursue creation of a personalized AI “superintelligence” that focuses on deep reasoning and long-horizon planning. The first model from this group, Muse Spark, is a multi-modal model able to digest and reason against text, images, video, audio, and even PDFs. It supports agents in long-running tasks. With the first release of the model in April, Meta boffins admitted in the announcement that they needed to work more on Spark’s coding abilities. The new 1.2 release addressed that deficiency. In another test, Muse Spark, running on Nvidia Hopper GPUs, tackled a kernel optimization task. Its agents made over 1,000 tool calls over a 24-hour period. “It kept finding substantial improvements well beyond the initial exploration phase,” Zuckerberg wrote. Understand the mission In his X missives, Zuckerberg included a somewhat vague chart comparing the performance of Muse Spark against other commercial models, using two industry benchmarks – Terminal-Bench 2.1 and DeepSWE 1.1 – that evaluate how autonomous agents act like software engineers, as well as a Meta Internal Coding bench too. The benchmarks all showed Muse Spark to be close to the best, but never the very best, at understanding the assigned engineering task and executing it with as little mission creep as possible. Muse Spark performed honorably compared to Opus 5, GPT5.6 Terra, Grok 4.5 and Gemini 3.6. The scores are tightly clustered, so they all did well (except occasionally Gemini, the current laggard du jour). So, Muse Spark is competitive anyway, though one eagle-eyed commenter wondered why OpenAI’s midline GPT5.6 Terra was used, instead of the top-tier GPT5.6 Sol. Installing the agent within your command line is possible through a curl command. Poly-model enthusiasts can also tap into Muse Spark via OpenRouter, or through its API. Muse Spark’s actual intelligence is metered at US$1.25 per million input tokens and US$4.25 per million output tokens. Discounts are available and the service offers a respectable 1 million token context window. ®

morning.title: An off-grid AI sounds like a great survival assistant, but is better left to roleplaying the zombie apocalypse
morning.text: OPINION In a post-apocalyptic setting – a zombie outbreak, for example – a small, off-grid language model running on something like a Raspberry Pi sounds like a survival cheat code. It’s certainly a clever way to get folks to check out your physical AI platform and maybe even splash out 7x the MSRP for an Nvidia Jetson Orin Nano with a battery enclosure, as one startup has done. But the scenario also sets a dangerous precedent, and in a real-world survival situation that local LLM could end up being a bigger liability than a lifesaver. Roleplaying a zombie apocalypse with a local AI model is harmless fun. Zombies aren’t real and you’re probably not LARPing your way through the backcountry pursued by the undead. The problem is there’s a certain group of people who are going to see the concept presented in videos like this and think an off-grid AI is a great idea for a bug-out bag or to bring along on a hiking trip, and it’s not hard to see why. Bit-for-bit, these models’ ability to retain information is unrivaled. You could download the entire English text of Wikipedia (about 24.7 GB compressed), and still not approach the information density of a four-billion-parameter model taking up 2 GB of memory. Add in vision capabilities, support for translation, and maybe layer in a few text-to-speech and speech-to-text models and it starts to sound like the perfect survival companion. But for reasons you have probably already experienced over the past four years, we wouldn’t recommend it. Even the largest LLMs still hallucinate — that is, they’ll confidently fabricate information and present it as fact. That’s because while models are trained on tens of trillions of words (really, tokens) of data, their ability to retrieve that data is inherently imperfect. LLMs don’t actually know what words belong together, just that statistically one word or another has the highest probability of coming next. It’s like auto-complete on steroids. Modern chatbots from OpenAI, Anthropic, or Google attempt to mitigate potential hallucinations by pulling in live web data to better inform their responses. The model is no longer answering your query on its own, but rather conducting research and presenting its findings. Even then, there’s no guarantee the information it retrieved is accurate or applicable to your specific context. Medical professionals have been sounding the alarm on the dangers of relying on LLMs for medical advice for some time now. According to OpenAI, more than 230 million people globally query ChatGPT with health and wellness related questions each week. The problem, medical professionals at Duke University School of Medicine note, is that these models can’t read between the lines to understand what the patient is really trying to say, and often suffer from sycophantic tendencies that lead them to tell users what they want to hear. “When a patient comes to us with a question, we read between the lines to understand what they’re really asking,” Ayman Ali, a fourth-year surgical resident at Duke Health, said in a blog post earlier this year. “We’re trained to interrogate the broader context. Large language models just don’t redirect people that way.” Off grid, an LLM can’t fall back on the web for help and almost certainly doesn’t benefit from the same guardrails that major chatbots use to protect users against potentially dangerous outputs. As we’ve shown time and time again, getting local LLMs running on inexpensive hardware has never been easier. For a contrived scenario like roleplaying a zombie apocalypse, the risk is minimal. But change things up and ask the model whether the berries pictured are edible, and you could be playing Russian roulette with a probability engine. ®
